searchText: eth2 networking call in 23.5 hours -- https://github.com/ethereum/eth2.0-pm/issues/137 <@!291925846556540928> in 13.5 probably? 13:00 UTC, right? 🙂 will you be recording the call <@!291925846556540928> ? <@!329594653097721856> yes, 13:00 UTC network call in 5 https://ethereumfoundation.zoom.us/j/861917128 I'll record the call locally and share on demand hit me up after Hey all! Question to clients: when doing initial sync (downloading and importing block by block), what block BLS validations do you perform? It seems that validating all the block BLS signatures (including attestations and randao) in all blocks seriously restricts the sync performance. My gut feeling is that while importing pretty large blocks chain (say several epochs +) validating just block signatures shouldn't mitigate security too much. Going further it could be sufficient to validate just a random subset of blocks (like it is done in Eth1 Fast sync: https://github.com/ethereum/go-ethereum/pull/1889). Notes from the networking call: https://hackmd.io/@benjaminion/rkEn7C_88 <@!425567222635954178> if you have a recently finalized piece of data you can effectively fast-forward to that block and then (hopefully) do a full verification of a much shorter chain (and possibly do a "full verification" of the chain in the background) a middle ground would be checking that there is in fact a hash chain from your genesis block to the recently finalized block Like <@!539495253418180618> says, If you do have a finalized root that you are syncing to, you could bypass most of the validation checks in the blocks prior. You cannot bypass any after. Another good technique to look into is using the "fast verification" trick across series of blocks instead of just within a single block (https://ethresear.ch/t/fast-verification-of-multiple-bls-signatures/5407). I think lighthouse has integrated this into their sync protocol Not sure that makes sense; the trick pretty quickly caps out at a fixed overhead reduction, especially if blocks are larger (and we should optimize our optimizations for the unhappy case) > the trick pretty quickly caps out at a fixed overhead reduction Interesting. Larger wrt number of signatures included? I'll let <@!361447803194441738> report on their experience from their testnet Correct me if I am wrong. Peer starts a sync to the most recent finalized checkpoint that belongs to the canonical view of the beacon chain. To justify whether suggested checkpoint is the one, in the first iteration peer gets a proof that the majority of peers in the network sharing this checkpoint as the most recent finalized one. In the second iteration the peer could observe the votes of the majority, if they are voting for the chain that is built upon that checkpoint then it must be the canonical one. But the second iteration is possible only when peer has access to the validator registry. So, the strategy would be as follows. Sync to the commonly shared finalized checkpoint in the network. Get a proof that validators keep voting on it and that their votes are valid. Won't it be secure enough to avoid checking any signatures prior to the finalized checkpoint? In general, by checking the signatures from the beginning, peer may be sure that it's syncing with the correct chain. But does it give a proof that this chain, even if it's correct, is the canonical one? Hello - how can one query the chain for a validator's place in the queue? Are there resources that I could be pointed to? Thank you. e.g. on the Prysm testnet Hi <@!615242182407880713>. I can help answer that. Prysm provides an API to query such data. Heres an example response: https://api.prylabs.net/eth/v1alpha1/validators/queue There is no validator in the activation queue at the moment. You can find more API endpoints at https://api.prylabs.net. I encourage you to join our discord channel if you have Prysm specific questions: https://discord.gg/YMVYzv6 Thanks!

excerpts.author: nashatyrev
excerpts.content:
Hey all! 
Question to clients: when doing initial sync (downloading and importing block by block), what block BLS validations do you perform? It seems that validating all the block BLS signatures (including attestations and randao) in all blocks seriously restricts the sync performance.

My gut feeling is that while importing pretty large blocks chain (say several epochs +) validating just block signatures shouldn't mitigate security too much. Going further it could be sufficient to validate just a random subset of blocks (like it is done in Eth1 Fast sync: https://github.com/ethereum/go-ethereum/pull/1889).

excerpts.author: djrtwo
excerpts.content:
Like <@!539495253418180618> says, If you do have a finalized root that you are syncing to, you could bypass most of the validation checks in the blocks prior. You cannot bypass any after.
Another good technique to look into is using the "fast verification" trick across series of blocks instead of just within a single block (https://ethresear.ch/t/fast-verification-of-multiple-bls-signatures/5407). I think lighthouse has integrated this into their sync protocol

excerpts.author: m.kalinin
excerpts.content:
Correct me if I am wrong. Peer starts a sync to the most recent finalized checkpoint that belongs to the canonical view of the beacon chain. To justify whether suggested checkpoint is the one, in the first iteration peer gets a proof that the majority of peers in the network sharing this checkpoint as the most recent finalized one. In the second iteration the peer could observe the votes of the majority, if they are voting for the chain that is built upon that checkpoint then it must be the canonical one. But the second iteration is possible only when peer has access to the validator registry.

So, the strategy would be as follows. Sync to the commonly shared finalized checkpoint in the network. Get a proof that validators keep voting on it and that their votes are valid. Won't it be secure enough to avoid checking any signatures prior to the finalized checkpoint?

excerpts.author: m.kalinin
excerpts.content: In general, by checking the signatures from the beginning, peer may be sure that it's syncing with the correct chain. But does it give a proof that this chain, even if it's correct, is the canonical one?
